claims.text: The initial material is an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy nanoalloy.
The initial nanoalloy has a homogeneous microstructure with nanoscale grain boundaries.
Preferential Mn oxidation is the primary cause of high-temperature structural and chemical instability in CrMnFeCoNi nanoalloys.
Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion drives the preferential oxidation of Mn.
Mn is transported along grain boundaries faster than the other constituent elements at elevated temperature.
Mn-mediated grain-boundary transport overrides the sluggish-diffusion benefit attributed to the high-entropy effect.
High-entropy alloys are designed to exhibit sluggish diffusion and chemical stability.
Mn is the major oxide-forming element in CrMnFeCoNi under both air and vacuum conditions.
Preferential Mn oxidation produces non-protective Mn-rich oxides.
Formation of Mn oxides depletes Mn from the bulk CrMnFeCoNi alloy.
Mn depletion undermines both structural integrity and chemical stability.
The proposed behavior occurs above 800 °C in both atmospheric and vacuum environments.
Standard CrMnFeCoNi nanoalloy samples will show substantial Mn depletion and non-protective Mn-oxide formation during high-temperature exposure.
Mn-oxide formation will be more pronounced in oxygen-rich environments.
Grain-boundary engineering can slow Mn diffusion in CrMnFeCoNi nanoalloys.
Slowing Mn diffusion through grain-boundary engineering will reduce Mn-oxide formation and Mn depletion relative to an unmodified baseline.
Reduced Mn oxidation and depletion will improve structural and chemical stability.
The prediction applies to nanoalloys with similar equiatomic compositions and nanoscale grain structures but may not apply to different compositions or phase-segregated states.

contradictions.description: The intervention and conditions specify testing under both air and vacuum, whereas the detailed falsification design specifies identical atmospheric conditions in air and does not clearly include a vacuum arm.
